title: The missed dose
topic: A colleague's error or poor performance
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in intensive care. At 08:00 you notice that Mr Gill, 70, who has septic shock, didn't receive his 06:00 dose of intravenous meropenem.

His nurse, Rob, says he was busy with another patient and will "catch it up" with the 10:00 drugs.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Ask the pharmacist how to adjust the timing of later doses.
options.brief: Helps get the dosing schedule right.
options.detailed: Giving a dose late may affect when the next one is due. The pharmacist can advise. It ranks second.

options.text: Ask Rob to give the missed dose straight away.
options.brief: Antibiotic timing matters in septic shock.
options.detailed: In septic shock, delays to antibiotics can affect outcome. Giving the dose now, rather than waiting two more hours, is safer. It ranks first.

options.text: Report Rob to the nurse in charge without speaking to him.
options.brief: Doesn't fix the dose, and bypasses a direct conversation.
options.detailed: The nurse in charge may need to know, but going straight to them without talking to Rob, and without dealing with the dose, is unhelpful.

options.text: Accept Rob's plan to give it at 10:00.
options.brief: Leaves a critically ill patient without antibiotics for longer.
options.detailed: A further two-hour delay in septic shock could cause harm. It is the least appropriate option.

options.text: Report the missed dose through the incident reporting system.
options.brief: Supports learning about workload and missed doses.
options.detailed: Missed doses often reflect workload problems. Reporting helps the unit look at why it happened. It ranks third.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you act on a colleague's omission that affects a critically ill patient, while staying constructive.
explanation.keyDetails: The patient is in septic shock. The dose is two hours late. The plan would make it four hours.
explanation.reasoning: [B] gets the dose given, [A] fixes the schedule, and [E] supports learning. [C] bypasses Rob and the patient's need, and [D] accepts a harmful delay.
explanation.competing: Some would report it before involving the pharmacist. The key prioritises getting his treatment right first.

references.title: Suspected sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management (NG51)
references.publisher: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 3, acting when patient safety is at risk.
